title: Pip's Lucky Ribbon Mission
markdown:
The Whispering Woods Annual Talent Show always made Pip the bunny’s fluffy fur droop and his long ears flatten. He got nervous just thinking about all the woodland creatures watching him. This year, he had to recite a poem about the dewdrop fairy. Standing alone on the big stage, under bright lights, made his tummy do flip-flops.

“It’s just a poem, Pip,” rumbled Marlo the mole, his best friend. “You’ve practiced so much! It’s a lovely poem.”

Pip sighed, his ears almost touching the floor of his burrow. “It’s not the poem, Marlo. It’s the stage and everyone watching. What if I forget my words? What if my voice sounds squeaky? What if I lose my lucky ribbon?” He patted his chest. His grandmother’s ribbon, spun from bravery itself, usually sat there.

Marlo patted Pip’s paw. “We’ll tie the ribbon tight. And if you’re still worried,” he winked, “I can dig a secret tunnel under the stage!”

Pip managed a weak smile. But that night, he remembered he’d left his ribbon backstage, near the velvet curtains, after adjusting his costume.

The next morning, cheerful music and the smell of acorn fritters floated through the trees. Pip’s stomach twisted. The show started in two hours, and his ribbon was gone!

“Marlo!” Pip whispered, hurrying to his friend’s burrow. “My ribbon! I left it backstage yesterday!”

Marlo’s whiskers twitched. “Backstage? That’s no problem! We’ll just pop in and grab it before anyone else arrives. Our secret mission!”

Pip gulped, his ears flattening. “Backstage? But it’s dark and quiet. The stage creaks, and the curtains look like big, sleepy ghosts.”

“Nonsense!” Marlo declared, puffing his chest. “Think of it as a pre-show adventure! We’ll be in and out as quick as a wink. My claws can help move things quietly!”

Under the soft dawn light, Pip and Marlo tiptoed to the festival tent. Marlo nudged the canvas flaps open, and they slipped inside. The air smelled of sawdust and old popcorn. It felt like a secret, magical place.

The hall was dim, with only dawn light peeking through. Long shadows danced, playing tricks on Pip’s eyes. The stage loomed ahead, a dark, silent platform. Heavy blue velvet curtains hung like giant, still caterpillars.

“Okay,” Pip whispered, his voice trembling. “Let’s find the ribbon and go. Very quietly.”

Marlo led the way, nudging a fallen cardboard turnip. Creak! The sound echoed, making Pip jump.

“Just a loose floorboard, Pip,” Marlo murmured. “Come on, brave explorers!”

They crept onto the stage. The wooden floorboards groaned softly. Pip imagined giants hiding underneath. Ropes dangled above like thick jungle vines. A painted backdrop of a moonlit forest swayed gently. To Pip’s wide eyes, it looked like a shimmering, see-through ghost.

“Oh, no!” Pip whimpered, freezing. “It’s a ghost! A stage ghost!”

Marlo peered up. “That’s not a ghost, Pip. That’s just painted scenery. Look!” He nudged a rope, making the “ghost” sway. “It’s just the breeze playing tricks. It’s not real.”

Pip saw the logic. It wasn’t a real ghost, just painted cloth. But his heart thumped like a drum. He scanned the dusty floor. Where was his ribbon? He remembered his costume basket was by the left wing, near a stack of wobbly crates.

“Over there!” Pip squeaked, pointing a shaky paw. “Near those crates!”

They shuffled towards the stage’s left side. Pip’s eyes darted. Shadows twisted like inky worms. The crates looked like a slumbering monster. A distant owl hooted like a warning.

Marlo sniffed the ground methodically. He paused near the edge of the stage.

“Aha!” Marlo rumbled triumphantly. He nudged a small, crumpled object with his snout. It was Pip’s lucky ribbon, its sunset colors a little dusty, but perfect.

Pip rushed forward, forgetting the creaks and shadows. He gently picked up the ribbon. It felt soft and familiar, like a warm hug. He looked around at the stage, the curtains, the swaying backdrop. He had walked onto this stage, faced his fears, and found his ribbon.

A warm feeling bubbled up inside Pip. It wasn’t nervousness anymore, but a happy glow. He looked at Marlo, who offered a proud smile.

“You did it, Pip,” Marlo said softly. “You were so brave.”

Pip carefully tied the ribbon around his neck. The knot felt snug and secure. He still felt a tiny twitch in his nose, but it was excitement now, not panic. He looked out at the empty seats, imagining the friendly faces that would soon fill them. The stage wasn’t scary anymore. It was just a stage. And he, Pip the bunny, was going to be on it. He took a deep, steady breath. He was ready.
characters: Pip the stage-fright bunny, Marlo the mole
